lesson.title: Cut Off Mid Sentence: Nonsense Mutations and Premature Stops
lesson.summary: A nonsense mutation changes a codon that specified an amino acid into a stop codon, ending protein synthesis early and usually producing a truncated, nonfunctional protein.
lesson.body:
The third possible outcome of a point mutation is the most abrupt. A nonsense mutation changes a codon that used to specify an amino acid into one of the three stop codons, UAA, UAG, or UGA, which the ribosome reads as an instruction to release the finished polypeptide rather than add another amino acid. The same worked example shows this outcome as well: changing the middle base of UCA, serine, from C to A produces UAA, a stop codon. Translation halts at that point instead of continuing to add the remaining amino acids the gene was supposed to encode.

The consequence of a nonsense mutation depends heavily on where in the gene it occurs. A premature stop codon near the very beginning of the coding sequence truncates almost the entire protein, which is essentially never functional. A premature stop codon very close to the normal, natural stop codon may remove only a handful of amino acids from the end of the protein, which can sometimes be tolerated if that region was not essential to folding or function. Between those extremes, the general rule holds: the earlier the premature stop, the more of the protein is missing, and the more likely the protein is to be nonfunctional or unstable.

Cells also have surveillance systems that respond to premature stop codons. In eukaryotic cells, an mRNA that contains a stop codon unusually far from its normal end is often recognized and degraded by a pathway called nonsense mediated decay before it is translated very much, which prevents the cell from wasting resources producing a truncated protein that is unlikely to be useful and might even interfere with the normal protein if it were made.

With silent, missense, and nonsense mutations all covered, the same starting codon, UCA for serine, has now shown all three fates a single point mutation can produce: no change at all when the substitution lands on a synonymous codon, a single altered amino acid when it lands on a codon for a different amino acid, and an early stop when it happens to create one of the three stop codons. All three are point mutations in the strictest sense, one base changed for another, yet their consequences range from completely unnoticed to potentially life threatening, which is exactly why the location and identity of a mutation matter as much as the fact that a mutation occurred at all.
